la:other:Cinna.html:
Cinna, ae, m.,
a family name of the gentes Cornelia and Helvia.
L. Cornelius Cinna, consul A.U.C. 667-670; a confederate of C. Marius in the Roman civil war with Sylla, ; ; and 55.—Hence, appel., a Cinna, a cruel warrior: tyrannum et Cinnam appellans, Dietsch.— Hence, Cinnānus, a, um, adj., of Cinna: partes,his party, adherents,; : rabies,: tumultus,.—
Son of the preceding of the same name, a follower of Lepidus, and afterwards one of the assassins of Cœsar, ; ; ; cf. .—
Cn. Cinna Magnus, son of the preceding, pardoned by Augustus, .—
C. Helvius Cinna, a Roman poet, friend of Catullus, the author of a poem, now lost, called Smyrna, ; ; ; ; ; ; ;

senses: to surround, circle, ring, encircle
to gird on; to crown or garland
la:verb:cingo.html:
cingo, xi, nctum, 3, v. a.
cf. Gr κυλλός, κυρτός; Lat. curvus, and clingo,
,
to go round in a circle, to surround, encompass, environ, gird, wreathe, crown, etc. (class. in prose and poetry).
Prop
In gen.: quid autem interius mente? Cingatur igitur corpore externo,i. e. it must be enclosed in a body,: non enim coronà consessus vester cinctus est, ut solebat,; cf.: judicium insolitā trepidum cinxere coronă,; tris (navīs) Eurus... Inhdit vadis atque aggere cingit harenae,: cincta serpentibus Hydra, id. ib 7, 658: pennae ritu coepere volucrum Cingere utrumque latus, to cover, Ov M. 6, 718, apio fasces et secto cingere porro, .—
Esp.
To surround the body with a girdle, to gird on (the sword), to gird; esp. freq in pass. with abl., to be girded, encircled with something. iam quasi zonā, liene cinctus ambulo, Plaut Curc. 2, 1, 5; ; cf.: cui lati clavi jus erit, ita cingatur, ut, etc.,: ut cingeretur fluxiore cincturā,: Hispano cingitur gladio,; ; : ferro,: ense, Ov F. 2, 13: cingor fulgentibus armis, Verg A. 2, 749; 11, 188, 11, 536; his cingi telis, id : ense latus cingit, Ov F. 2, 784; cf. : cinctas resolvite vestes, Ov M. 1, 382. filios balteis,.—Poet., in pass with acc. (cf. accingor, II., and Zumpt, Gr § 458): inutile ferrum Cingitur,: cinctaeque ad pectora vestes Bracchia docta movent, Ov M. 6, 59.—Without case: Syrinx, Ov M. 1, 695; puer alte cinctus,.—Hence, in late Lat. cinctus = armis instructus, armatus, armed, equipped, enrolled: cinctus in aliā militiā,; cf. .—As a girding up of the Roman dress was necessary in pursuits requiring physical action, hence, cingor (cf accingor), to make one's self ready for any thing, to prepare: cingitur, certe expedit se,; cingitur ipse furens certatim in proelia Turnus,; cf. supra,; Hor S. 2, 8, 10; .—
To encircle with a garland or crown, to crown (freq., esp in the poets).
Of the head: muralique caput summum cinxere coronā,; cf. Ov A. A. 3, 392 tempora floribus,; Verg A. 5, 71: spicis, et saep.: comam lauro,; cf.: Graias barbara vitta comas,; : de tenero cingite flore caput, Ov F 3, 254.—Poet.: Atlantis, cinctum assidue cui nubibus atris Piniferum caput et vento pulsatur et imbri,; ; .—
To encircle other parts of the body: cujus lacertos anuli mei cingant,.—
Of places, to surround, encircle, invest, enclose (the prevailing signif. in prose, esp. in the histt.; syn.: circumdo, claudo): (Tellus) oras maris undique cingens, ; ; : flumen Dubis paene totum oppidum cingit, provincia mari cincta, : urbe portus ipse cingitur et continetur, Zumpt: quod moenibus cingebatur,: quae (terra) magnā ex parte cingitur fluctibus, speciem insulae praebet, etc.,; ; Ov A. A. 2, 469: cingitur insula tribus millibus passuum, i.e. has a circuit of, etc., .—Poet.: cinxerunt aethera nimbi,covered,: medium diem cinxere tenebrae,.—Trop.; diligentius urbem religione quam ipsis moenibus cingitis,fortify,.—
In milit. lang., to surround a place or army for defence or in a hostile manner, to fortify, to invest, be set, besiege: coronā militum cincta urbs,: castra vallo, id 7, 39, 8 equites cornua cinxere. covered, : ultimum agmen validā manu,to cover,: urbem obsidione,to besieye,; dextera cingitur amni,: (hostem) stationibus in modum obsidii,: cingi ab armis hostium,; , .—Trop Sicilia multis undique cincta persons. Cio. Imp. Pomp 11, 30.—
To escort, to accompany inermi item regi praetor Achaeorum et unus ex purpuratis latus cingebant, Liv 32, 39, 8: dum latus sancti cingit tibi turba senatus, Ov P. 4, 9, 17: nec noscitur ulli, Agminibus comitum qui mode cinctus erat,: cincta virgo matrum catervā, id M. 12, 216, Vell 2, 14, 1,; Sil 4, 448,—
To peel off the bark around: cingere est deglabrare, Pr, cf. Plin 17, 24, 37, § 234 sqq.

la:noun:cinis.html:
cĭnis, ĕris, m. (in
sing. fem., ; ; ; Caesar, acc. to ; Calvus ap. Non. l. l. and ap. Charis; p. 78 p; ; Scrib. c. 226; 230; 232; 245, Ser. c. 44; ; Inscr. Orell 4479; cf. Neue, Formenl. 1, p. 657; access. form: hoc cĭnus, Gloss. Labb.; Sicul. Flacc. p. 140, 17,; p. 308, 5; cf. Lachm. ad Lucr 2, p. 190, and a nom.cĭ-ner is mentioned by : 6, p. 707) [kindr with κόνις; cf. also naucus], ashes,
In gen. (while favilla is usually the ashes that is light like dust, or is still glowing; cf.: corporis favillam ab reliquo separant cinere,: cinis e

favillā et carbonibus ad calfaciendum triclinium illatis exstinctus et jam diu frigidus exarsit repente, ), ; cf. , and 4, 927; Cato ap. P.; ; ; ; ; .—

From the use of ashes for scouring vessels, the proverb is derived: hujus sermo haut cinerem quaeritat,. —
Esp.
The ashes of a corpse that is burned; so very freq. in both numbers; in plur. esp. freq. in the poets and postAug. prose.
In sing.: cur hunc dolorem cineri ejus atque ossibus inussisti?: ex tuā calamitate cinere atque ossibus filii sui solacium reportare,, § 128: dare poenas cineri atque ossibus clarissimi viri,: obsecravit per fratris sui mortui cinerem, (cf. in plur.: jura per patroni tui cineres,); ; ; ; ; ; 11, 211; ; ; ; .— Poet. for death, or the person after death: Troja virūm et virtutum omnium acerba cinis,: et cedo invidiae, dummodo absolvar cinis,i. e. after my death,: et mea cum mutuo fata querar cinere,: nunc non cinis ille poëtae Felix?: post cinerem (after burning the corpse) cineres haustos ad pectora pressant, .—Figuratively: cineri nunc medicina datur,i. e. when it is too late,—
In plur., ; : expedit matris cineres opertos Fallere,; ; ; Suet, Calig. 15; ; ; —
The ruins of a city laid waste and reduced to ashes: cineres patriae,: patriae cinis,; cf. .—
Trop., an emblem of destruction, ruin, annihilation: si argentum'st, omne id ut fiat cinis,: quicquid erat nactus praedae majoris, ubi omne Verterat in fumum et cinerem,i. e. had consumed, spent,; cf. ; .

Concr., a girdle, belt: cinctus et cingulum a cingendo, alterum viris, alterum mulieribus attributum, Müll., cf. (in good prose, although not in Cic.); ; ; , ; .
